questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted something with new environments and nature to see, great opportunities for travel, a majority of English speakers and relatively good academic status for the university itself.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. Easier than my home university if I am being honest. They do a pretty good job of letting you know the basics in the intro week, so make sure to make it to a few of the events there, also to meet new people. They also have an extensive academic support network that is usually always accessible, right on campus, if you have any questions.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Intro week, emails of good info, as well as a welcome package in the airport with a prepaid sim which was very helpful!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Colleges, although they are quite expensive, they are easy to apply for and they also provide meals. This makes for similar costs of living when compared with finding a sharehouse or apartment. I chose trinity college, which was the second cheapest on college row, but cheaper options feature no AC in the rooms (probably miserable during summer) and less social events (so i heard, but take it with a grain of salt) and I was quite happy with trinity overall.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Most colleges have a dining hall with regular meals. The meals at trinity can be a little stale at times, but they are good enough and I very rarely skipped a meal.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It is expensive, and most of the colleges are right next to a busy road, so if you want something quieter and cheaper, it may be better to go looking for other accommodation options by yourself. UWA partners with other options in the city centre if you want to apply through them, but want less of college life. College is a good way to meet people however and I enjoyed it for that reason especially.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Relatively straightforward, but the visa is quite daunting and expensive (about 1000 euros), which may be intended for longer academic stays. Don't get too scared by all the questions in the visa (like I did) as they usually approve them immediately and just set aside a good amount of time to complete it and get familiar with the required documents, so you can obtain them before the deadline of submission.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: UWA has a website and email for enquiries which they usually answer quite quick. Aside from that, the welcome letter contained a good bit of info and you can also register for a pre-departure zoom session where they take you through most of what you need to do, which I recommend. Most of the info is on the exchange part of the UWA site, so have a good read through that.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all 4 of the ones i wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Prepare a good few months in advance to avoid too much stress. Moving to a new country will be daunting, but take it one step at a time and you'll make it through the process. Once you're there you sort of forget the application process and it's minor perils.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Most of my lecturers were quite good, with just a few duds. However, be prepared for much more mandatory coursework and small assignments that are surprisingly time-consuming. Don't be afraid to apply for extensions if you want to make travel plans around schoolwork, the unit coordinators are usually generous with these.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took one first year course, one second year course and two third year courses, but you can definitely make it easier or harder for yourself by selecting other courses. I found that this level was just about what I could fit in and I would have loved less work to do at times:

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: A bit more memorizing to do and a less intuitive and rhetorical approach than what one may be used to in danish education, closer to an "American" way of teaching. This does differ between courses though.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: I took Plants in action, Neuroscience in society, Clean, green & ethical animal production and Ecological processes.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Neuroscience in society and ecological processes were my favourites. Lecturers were passionate and the courses well structured and expectations reasonable. Especially ecological processes taught me a lot.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Opening a bank account, although this was not necessary. Visa was also very expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: General amenities and food were quite expensive as there weren't really any equivalents to budget stores like Rema 1000 or Netto. Coles was the cheapest option for groceries and for bigger items and accessories go to kmart.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sport and lots of clubs! They do an orientation day early in the semester with a booth for every club and sport opportunity, so go there if you want an overview of the options. Most of these are also basically free to participate in. I personally joined the rollerblading club and bought my own pair of blades which was great fun. Rolling to class in the mornings definitely made the semester that much better and the campus is quite clean of debris and full of little spots to jump.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join a club or a sport.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Use the bigger study breaks and the time after exams to do roadtrips, north and south! North is best to do in the australian winter/spring as it is still very warm at that time and will likely be too hot during summer, where the south is more appealing. Exmouth and Karijini national park were highlights, offering great snorkeling and captivating desert respectively. The desert is highly recommended as it is just so exotic and peaceful. Me and a friend managed to get a van incredibly cheap through a relocation company, so look into that if you want to save money, although it does come with certain restrictions, so read the fine print. Other than that Perth has great bush parks and beaches and quite a few snorkel/diving spots. If you have an advanced divers license, the UWA underwater club offers pretty cheap dives throughout the semester, so check that out.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. Australians are very welcoming and easygoing, although there may be some slang to get used to. A lot of Australian also get up quite early in the morning and go to bed earlier than in europe, which makes for shorter nights out on the town if that's your thing. I personally found this quite nice and that I got more sleep than back home, also helped by the close proximity to campus of course.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Do the intro events at the start of the semester, even you feel a little tired or stressed. Talk to people at uni after class if you get the chance and if you live at a college, don't be afraid to join new people at their meals in the dining hall. Talking to the locals will get you great tips for things to do and see and you'll get to know a bit more about the culture, making your stay much better.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Uni students are generally a bit younger than in Denmark and at a college you might live with people who are as young as 18, so be prepared for some occasional gaps in maturity when talking to other students. This mostly affects the vibe of social functions where people tend to drink a lot more unrestrained. I found that most Australians I met at uni were between 19-21 of age.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness and lack of formalities. They take some getting used to, but after a while you might find that your shoulders drop a bit.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Explore the nature as much as you can, spend time with locals and go to the beach, even when you assignments due.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Consider getting a car with friends and get a smartrider card to save money on public transport.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The nature and the experience of self-reliance while living in another country. Hiking the cape to cape track and doing roadtrips were great experiences and I can highly recommend.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding enough time for everything and battling the inevitable FOMO.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
